etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English frown, froun (“a threatening appearance; lowering of the clouds”), from frounen (“to frown”). See below.

definitions.definition: A wrinkling of the forehead with the eyebrows brought together, typically indicating displeasure, severity, or concentration.

quote.citation: 1860, George Eliot, “V: Maggie's Second Visit”, in The Mill on the Floss‎[1], Volume I Book II, Edinburgh, London: William Blackwood, page 336‑337:
quote.text: Philip had once told him of a man who had a horse-shoe frown, and Tom had tried with all his frowning-might to make a horse-shoe on his forehead

quote.citation: 1873, Charles Darwin, The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals‎[2], page 223:
quote.text: He encounters some obstacle in his train of reasoning ... and then a frown passes like a shadow over his brow.

definitions.definition: (Canada, US) A downturn of the corners of the mouth, typically expressing sadness.

quote.citation: 1911 December, “Facial Expression Electric Sign”, in Popular Electricity‎[3], volume iv, number 8, Chicago, page 714:
quote.text: The smile and the frown are both indicated and the operation of a motor driven flasher causes the face to look happy and sad in turn.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English frounen (“to frown as an expression of disapproval, displeasure, shame, fear, or jealousy”), from Old French frognier (“to frown or scowl”), from Gaulish *frognā (“nostril”), from Proto-Celtic *srognā.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To have a frown on one's face.
(intransitive, figurative) To manifest displeasure or disapprobation; to look with disfavour or threateningly.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii]:
quote.text: The sky doth frown and lower upon our army.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To repress or repel by expressing displeasure or disapproval; to rebuke with a look.

quote.citation: 2017 June 26, Alexis Petridis, “Glastonbury 2017 verdict: Radiohead, Foo Fighters, Lorde, Stormzy and more”, in the Guardian‎[4]:
quote.text: As the band paused between songs, a gust of wind blew a distinctive Worthy Farm odour in the direction of drummer/vocalist Julien Ehrich: “Wow,” he frowned, “this place smells of cow shit.”
